title: From election integrity to wealth taxes, voters to decide key ballot measures
text:
From election integrity to wealth taxes, voters to decide key ballot measures
On Election Day, voters in 39 U.S. states will weigh in on more than 140 ballot measures.
As the United States gears up for midterm elections Nov. 3, voters are weighing not just the balance of power in Congress, but also a host of issues in state ballot measures. In 39 states, the public will decide 145 such measures, in which people vote directly on changes to state laws or constitutions.
Ballot measures often reflect local issues in each state, says John Matsusaka, executive director of the Initiative and Referendum Institute at the University of Southern California. But sometimes, “there are issues ... that happen at the national level that spark a response across multiple states.”
That dynamic is playing out this year, with many ballot measures reflecting policies that have taken center stage during President Donald Trump’s second term. More than 15 states are mulling changes to how they conduct elections, including some that might revise their redistricting rules or congressional maps. Others are considering measures on campaign financing and initiatives targeting noncitizen voting.
On Election Day, voters in states across the U.S. will weigh in on ballot measures addressing significant policy questions. While some are local matters, others reflect a response to national issues.
Also on the ballot are initiatives focused on abortion, transgender rights, and wealth taxes. Here’s a look at some of this year’s most consequential ballot measures.
Voting rights and redistricting
Voters in Alaska, Kansas, South Dakota, West Virginia, Arizona, and Arkansas will weigh whether to amend state laws or constitutions to explicitly bar noncitizens from voting, even though federal and state laws already state that only U.S. citizens can vote in national and state elections.
President Trump has claimed for years that U.S. elections are beset with fraud, including widespread noncitizen voting. Data shows there is no evidence that noncitizens vote in numbers large enough to influence elections, or that elections in general see meaningful fraud.
Residents in Arizona, California, Nevada, North Carolina, and Ohio will also consider whether to require government-issued or photo identification to vote – another policy favored by Mr. Trump.
Partisan redistricting of congressional districts has emerged as another key fight on ballots, following a rush of mid-decade map drawing this year.
- Missourians will decide whether a congressional map that could grant Republicans an additional House seat can go into effect.
- A measure in Colorado could make mid-decade redistricting harder by requiring the state’s Supreme Court and an independent commission to approve those maps.
- Maryland’s citizens, by contrast, could make partisan gerrymandering easier by amending the constitution to exempt congressional maps from the state’s redistricting criteria.
Campaign finance
A handful of ballot measures this cycle aim to clamp down on campaign contributions, but they take different tacks on whose money to regulate. The policies could prove popular across the aisle: Almost three-quarters of Americans polled by Politico this spring agreed that “there is too much money in American politics.”
Most significant among the measures is one in Montana, where voters could ban donations from “artificial persons” such as corporations, nonprofits, and trusts. The measure would directly contradict the Supreme Court’s landmark 2010 ruling, Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission, which remade American politics by opening it to corporate spending.
An initiative in Michigan would ban contributions from certain electric and gas utilities, as well as from any entity holding state contracts exceeding $250,000 per year.
Abortion
Ballot initiatives in Nevada and Virginia would enshrine abortion access by constitutional amendment.
Nevada law already allows abortion until the 24th week of pregnancy, but this year’s ballot measure would codify similar provisions in the state constitution, making them harder to repeal. Constitutional amendments in Nevada become valid only after they pass in two consecutive general elections. The current measure passed with 64% of the vote in 2024. An initiative in Virginia, where abortion is legal until the end of the second trimester, would similarly make the procedure a constitutional right.
Missourians, by contrast, will decide whether to ban the procedure with very few exceptions. Should Missouri’s Amendment 3 pass, it would rescind a 2024 constitutional amendment that allows abortion until fetal viability. This year’s ballot measure would ban the procedure except in cases of “medical emergency, fetal anomaly, rape, or incest.” In cases of rape or incest, abortion would be illegal after 12 weeks.
In Idaho, which has one of the strictest abortion bans in the country, a ballot measure would legalize the procedure until fetal viability, or in medical emergencies, via state statute.
Transgender rights
Five states will consider ballot measures restricting transgender minors’ access to medical treatments for gender transitions or transgender athletes’ ability to play on teams matching their self-declared gender identity.
- Measures in Arizona, Nebraska, Washington, and Colorado would require student-athletes to play on teams that match their sex at birth.
- In Arizona, Nebraska, and Colorado, the rules would apply to K-12 schools and colleges; in Washington, they would apply only to primary schools. Washington’s rules would also require those who play on female teams to undergo sex verification, a controversial policy that can involve a physical exam.
A second measure in Colorado would prohibit gender-transition surgery for minors. Missouri’s Amendment 3, in addition to implementing an abortion ban, would outlaw gender-transition surgery or hormone replacement therapy for children under age 18 seeking to change their sex.
Wealth and income taxes
In California, voters could levy a one-time 5% tax on billionaires. Revenue from the tax would fund healthcare, food assistance, and public education. California’s Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates the tax would raise tens of billions of dollars in the short term, but could push out some of the state’s billionaires, leading to a long-term decrease in annual revenue by rates of less than $1 billion per year.
Colorado’s Initiative 195 takes a different approach. It would replace the state’s flat 4.4% income tax with a progressive tax, with rates that rise from 3.7% to 8.4% depending on income. That would lower taxes for the state’s lowest earners, but nearly double them for the highest earners. The measure is competing with an opposing initiative that would cap the income tax at its current rate. Under Colorado law, when two conflicting ballot measures pass, the one with the most “yes” votes prevails.
Measures taxing rich people have picked up steam as income inequality has widened and politicians attempt to combat rising costs. But they’ve also inspired opposition.
A ballot measure in Washington, backed by a local hedge fund manager, would eliminate the state’s recently passed 9.9% tax on household incomes exceeding $1 million. The state’s Office of Financial Management estimates that, should the initiative pass, it would result in an $11.4 billion revenue loss for the state over five fiscal years.
